items.title: DeepFine to Lead Development of Industrial AI Agent Technology for Manufacturing Logistics - thelec.net
items.summary: According to DeepFine, the project aims to develop industrial AI agents capable of analyzing diverse
items.content:
According to DeepFine, the project aims to develop industrial AI agents capable of analyzing diverse operational data generated on factory floors and assisting workers with task execution and decision-making. The system will combine smart glasses, computer vision AI, large language models (LLMs), and edge computing technologies to improve efficiency across logistics processes ranging from inventory management and picking operations to outbound shipments.

Workers using smart glasses will receive real-time guidance on materials to be shipped, required quantities, and workflow sequences. Vision AI will identify materials and verify that workers have selected the correct items, immediately alerting them to potential errors to improve operational accuracy. [...] The company also plans to implement an LLM-based AI agent capable of providing voice-based assistance directly on the factory floor. Workers will be able to ask questions during operations and receive responses based on real-time operational and production data, eliminating the need to stop work or consult separate devices.

DeepFine said the edge computing architecture was designed to meet the stringent security requirements of manufacturing environments. Video and operational data generated on-site will be processed locally rather than transmitted to external cloud infrastructure, enabling AI deployment even in facilities where connections to external networks are restricted.

As for regional and smaller players in the market, Armstrong said a lot of them are getting acquired, which he said is a clear trend, with demand still there, albeit having softened.

A bigger issue, he observed, is that available labor is somewhat scarce, as it has become more difficult to find independent contractors, both on the driver side and the provider side, which is forcing more freight brokerage usage as well. [...] Findings for the report, entitled “Recalibrating: Big and Bulky Last-Mile Delivery in the United States-2026,” were based on two separate studies and also public information, with surveys sent to NHDA members and other U.S. last-mile delivery 3PLs, with 2025 last-mile delivery revenues of 3PLs coming in between $1.5 million-to-$1.2 billion, accounting for 33% of the estimated $10.63 billion U.S. Third-Party Logistics Big and Bulky Last-Mile Delivery Market.

In the report, Armstrong & Associates estimated that from 2017 to 2025, the market grew at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.6%, and called for a 5.1% CAGR from 2025 through 2027, coming in at an estimated $11.42 billion in 2026 and $12.34 billion in 2027. [...] “What happened with tariffs was an overall headwind,” said Armstrong. “You started having more ocean and air consolidations, so a lot of it happened at the point of origin versus the point of delivery. # Israeli cybersecurity firm Vega launches open AI threat detection standard

## Vega publicly released the framework through DetectionSkills.io and GitHub ahead of Black Hat USA 2026 in Las Vegas, where the company is demonstrating the technology.

Follow us on Google

Cyber security and cybercrime alert

(photo credit: FAMILY STOCK)

ByJERUSALEM POST STAFF

Israeli cybersecurity company Vega announced on Tuesday the launch of Detection Skills, an open standard designed to help security teams capture, share, and automate the reasoning used by experienced defenders to detect and investigate cyber threats. [...] The framework, which is available to companies regardless of whether they use Vega’s products, combines threat detection, alert triage, investigation, and continuous improvement into reusable AI-powered workflows.

Vega publicly released the framework through DetectionSkills.io and GitHub ahead of Black Hat USA 2026 in Las Vegas, where the company is demonstrating the technology.

Traditional cybersecurity systems have generally relied on detection rules that identify previously recognized patterns of malicious activity. Vega said this approach has become harder to maintain as artificial intelligence allows attackers to develop and alter their techniques more rapidly. [...] “Detection Skills answer with scaled AI reasoning that brings the judgment of your best cyber defense engineers to every alert, in real time,” he added. “We made the standard open to ensure the whole industry rises with it: As attacks scale, defense compounds.”

Vega said the framework does not make changes to an organization’s systems without human approval. Security engineers retain access to the AI’s reasoning, including the information it reviewed and the basis for its decisions.

The framework was built on the Agent Skills concept originally developed by artificial intelligence company Anthropic and adapted specifically for cybersecurity operations.

items.summary: As agentic AI becomes more ingrained in enterprise infrastructure, the attack surface it creates rem
items.content:
As agentic AI becomes more ingrained in enterprise infrastructure, the attack surface it creates remains largely uncharted. Research like this is how the community stays ahead: every privilege escalation path surfaced and every detection shipped is one less blind spot for the people defending real environments.

## Explore More Research from Phantom Labs

The research highlighted in this piece is only a fraction of what Phantom Labs uncovered this year:

 Claude & Control: An Introduction to Agentic C2 with Computer Use Agents
 A Security Researcher’s Guide to Understanding Copilot Studio AI Agents
 From Heuristics to Histograms: Reinventing Kerberoasting Detections
 Pwning AI Code Interpreters in AWS Bedrock AgentCore [...] The team’s research spanned cloud AI platforms (58% of all AI/LLM research), AI agents and agentic systems (42%), model and data security (12%), prompt injection/jailbreak (9%), and AI-specific privilege escalation (6%). In one case, the team showed how an AWS AgentCore agent's inherited permissions could be escalated into broader account access. This is a concrete example of how AI, even in trusted infrastructure, have privilege models customers need to monitor and control.

## Theme 2: Visibility Without Context Isn’t Enough [...] AI agents are rapidly becoming another class of enterprise identity, authenticating to systems, invoking tools, accessing data, inheriting permissions, and acting autonomously on behalf of users. As organizations deploy more agents across cloud, SaaS, and internal workflows, they create new identity relationships and privilege escalation paths that security teams must discover and govern.

Now everyone thinks they're behind. AI is creating the same comparison trap that social media created years ago. With AI becoming broader every day, trying to master everything is a losing strategy.

## AI Is Exposing, Not Creating, The Future Of Work [...] another AI model
 another announcement

 another prediction
 another headline

Employees don't feel behind because they're learning slowly. They feel behind because the finish line keeps moving. The learning curve seems endless and unmanageable.

### AI Is Sparking a Fear of Becoming Obsolete

This fear is different from job loss. Many professionals aren't worried about unemployment as much as they're worried about becoming irrelevant. No one wants to become the reluctant relic. Becoming obsolete is emotionally different from losing your job. People are thinking: I still have my job, but am I being marked down?

### Comparison Culture

Another growing issue is the fear of falling behind peers. Look at your LinkedIn feed or other social media. There are endless posts like: [...] Media attention exploded in January and February 2023, and the initial news coverage sent a clear message: You will be replaced. Then, coverage increased after Microsoft integrated ChatGPT into Bing and Google announced Bard. From that point onward, there was a steady stream of headlines about job displacement, misinformation, hallucinations, and existential AI risk. Recently, though, AI leaders and economists have changed their minds about the scope of the disruption. But the fear persists.

items.summary: We are also only at the front end of AI diffusion into the real economy. We have not yet seen the fu
items.content: We are also only at the front end of AI diffusion into the real economy. We have not yet seen the full impact of AI capabilities in a hyperconnected environment where massive volumes of data from factory floors, hospitals, farms, homes, and even our bodies are captured by sensors, processed on‑device and at the edge, fed into models for training and refinement, and then pushed back into physical systems in the real world—all riding on AI‑native 6G, cloud, and edge infrastructure. That trajectory implies a technological future that will demand vast amounts of cost‑efficient compute—and one in which today’s cybersecurity and data‑protection challenges pale in comparison to the far more consequential risks to critical infrastructure, sovereign control over data, and systems integrity. [...] Energy reform agenda remains jammed while China retains the power advantage. Power availability becomes an effective cap on US and allied AI buildouts. Congressional gridlock keeps permitting reforms in a logjam, state and local pushback to data center growth constrain additional policy support, and supply chain bottlenecks compound the challenge of bringing new power supply online. Advanced nuclear, geothermal, long-duration storage, carbon capture, and next-generation grid technologies need pooled, bloc-scale demand and patient capital to move down the cost curve, but fragmented and competing policies across US and partner countries prevent these projects from reaching commercial scale. Allied manufacturing capacity for grid equipment expands too slowly to relieve the bottlenecks, while [...] Ex-China diversification agenda loses steam. The US leans heavily on unilateral tariffs with minimal carveouts that end up hurting partners as much as China in the early years. By 
Ian Duncan

The White House told top technology companies Tuesday that it would exempt certain artificial intelligence systems from its plans for government vetting of new AI models, giving free tools known as “open weight” models a pass and focusing scrutiny on the latest technology from leading U.S. companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.
